Compare Fit Statistics Between Two OLS Models from Multiply-Imputed SCF Data

Source: R/scf_compare_ols.R
scf_compare_ols.Rd

scf_compare_ols() compares two OLS regression models estimated using scf_ols(), focusing on their relative model fit. It reports the difference in AIC and R-squared values across multiply-imputed implicates to help evaluate whether the added variables in a more complex model meaningfully improve explanatory power.

scf_compare_ols(mod1, mod2)

Arguments

mod1

The baseline model (typically the simpler or nested model), estimated with scf_ols().

mod2

The comparison model (typically more complex), also from scf_ols().

Value

No return value. This function prints the difference in AIC (\\Delta AIC) and R-squared (\\Delta R²) to the console.

Details

The function is designed for model comparison workflows involving multiply-imputed Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF) data. Because standard likelihood ratio tests cannot be applied to multiply-imputed regressions, this function uses changes in AIC and R² as pragmatic substitutes.

In multiply-imputed settings, log-likelihoods are not pooled across implicates, so formal likelihood ratio tests are not well-defined. Instead, researchers typically compare model fit by evaluating:

  • \Delta AIC: A drop of 2–4 suggests weak evidence for the more complex model; 5–10 is moderate; 10+ is strong.

  • \Delta R²: Provides a descriptive indication of how much more variance is explained by the comparison model.

AIC and R² values are extracted from model attributes set by scf_ols(). This function assumes that both models were estimated using the same number of implicates and that they are applied to the same data.

Example Interpretation

If \\Delta AIC = -12.3 and \\Delta R² = 0.02, the more complex model shows a moderate improvement in fit and explains an additional 2% of the variance in the outcome variable.

See also

scf_ols(), scf_fit_ols() for inspecting model diagnostics, scf_update() for preparing variables.

Examples

if (FALSE) { # \dontrun{
model_a <- scf_ols(scf2022, log(networth) ~ age)
model_b <- scf_ols(scf2022, log(networth) ~ age + income + factor(edcl))
scf_compare_ols(model_a, model_b)
} # }
